newsitem.title: singapore: Asia-Europe talks promise more links, avoid issues.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Europe talks promise more links, avoid issues.

text.p: Foreign ministers from 25 Asian and European countries wrapped up four days of talks on Saturday promising stronger links covering all fields of human endeavour.
But the talks, described by Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo as "symbolising friendship", sidestepped most divisive issues and were overshadowed by a series of heavyweight bilateral meetings.

The Chinese and South Korean foreign ministers met to discuss a diplomatic crisis over a North Korean defector holed up in Seouls embassy in Beijing, while British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind appeared preoccupied with Hong Kong.
He left early for the British colony which is due to be handed back to China at the end of June, cutting slightly short an Asian tour to fly home to London for a parliamentary vote.
But the chairman of the two-day Asia-Europe Meeting (ASEM), Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar, said the talks were "highly productive".

"Asia-Europe cooperation should be multi-faceted, encompassing all fields of human endeavour, including economics, politics, culture, educations, environment and science and technology," he said in a statement.

The ASEM followed a conference between the European Union (EU) and the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) earlier this week that was marked by frank exchanges over human rights, especially on Burma.
Burma is due to join ASEAN -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- possibly as early as this year.
Japan, China and South Korea joined ASEAN on the Asian side for the ASEM talks with the 15-member European Union to prepare for a second Asia-Europe summit due in London next April.
Burma, whose top officials are banned from Europe, could be a problem unless a solution is found before the London summit.
But Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi said no final decision on new ASEM members was likely to be made until the London summit.
"I do not anticipate at the moment a decision being taken earlier than at the summit in London," he told reporters. That could avoid embarassment over visas for Burmese delegates.
Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn told reporters the EU wanted Southeast Asia to put pressure on Burmas military rulers to improve their human rights record.
Southeast Asia would use "every which way" to bring Burma into line with international standards, but Europe should act because it "shared responsibility", he said.

He said the EU should press pro-democracy campaigner Aung San Suu Kyi to drop calls for sanctions against Burmas State Law and Order Restoration Council, which seized power in 1988 and ignored the results of subsequent elections her party won.
Delegates said Burma was not specifically discussed at Saturdays conference, which focused more on how to talk about the issues than the issues themselves.
Jayakumar said the ministers had agreed the Asia-Europe talks could be widened in future to include more countries.
Japanese Foreign Affairs spokesman Hidehiko Hamada told a news conference there was "not much objection" to membership for Australia, New Zealand, India and Pakistan.
"There was almost emerging a consensus as far as the Asian countries were concerned," Hamada said.
Jayakumar said the ASEM talks filled a gap in global diplomacy: "The weak link in this triangular relationship was between Asia and Europe."
Throughout the four days, Asian delegates complained the Europeans were more interested in talking about political issues than trade liberalisation, which is the Asian priority.
European delegates said a political dimension was important. "The Asians want to have the economic cooperation and the technology transfer without all the lectures," one said.
Van Mierlo noted the ASEM talks began over dinner on Valentines Day, February 14:
"This was, of course, a very lucky coincidence because our meeting is meant to symbolise friendship."
